result.summary: Pausanias lists the notable sights of Epidaurus, then turns to the island of Ægina, giving its early history, the genealogy of Æacus's descendants and the later fortunes of the Æginetans. He describes the Hall of Æacus and the drought story behind its statues, the tomb of Phocus and how Peleus killed him, and the island's theatre.

scenes.title: Sights of Epidaurus
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the temples and statues of Epidaurus, including those of Æsculapius, Dionysus, Artemis, Aphrodite, Hera and Athene.

scenes.title: History of Ægina
scenes.summary: Ægina is settled by men Zeus made from the soil. The text traces the descendants of Æacus and Phocus and the island's later rise and fall.
scenes.stakes: The Æginetans risk losing their island and power to Athens.

scenes.title: Ægina and the Hall of Æacus
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the island's dangerous approaches and the Hall of Æacus. The statues commemorate the envoys who begged Æacus to end a drought.
scenes.stakes: Greece suffers drought until Æacus intercedes with Zeus.

scenes.title: Death of Phocus
scenes.summary: At the tomb of Phocus, Pausanias tells how Peleus killed him with a quoit. Telamon's attempt to defend himself from a mole fails and he sails back to Salamis.
scenes.stakes: Telamon and Peleus face exile and guilt for murder.

scenes.title: The Theatre
scenes.summary: A theatre near the harbour Secret resembles the one at Epidaurus, with a stadium wall supporting it.

alias_notes.explanation: Local epithet of Athene for her wooden statue at Epidaurus.
Epithet of Zeus as god of all Greeks, worshipped on Ægina.
Old name of the island, replaced by the name of Asopus's daughter.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias remarks on Ægina's famously dangerous approaches, a rare comment on its geography.

analysis.text: The chapter links sights to local legends and genealogies, showing how Greek places preserved memory through monuments, tombs and descent.
Æginetan naval power, its expulsion by Athens and later recovery reflect real rivalries of the fifth century BC.

fun_facts.text: The Epidaurus theatre, which Pausanias uses as a comparison, is still in use for performances today.

language_notes.text: Cissæan is an epithet of Athene, probably from Cissus (ivy); the text only says this is what the locals call the statue.
Zeus carried off Ægina, daughter of the river-god Asopus; their son was Æacus. The island's old name Œnone means 'wine-land'.
Peleus and Telamon, sons of Æacus, killed their half-brother Phocus and were exiled; Peleus fathered Achilles, Telamon fathered Ajax.
Miltiades and Cimon, Athenian leaders, traced their descent to Ajax's family; Miltiades commanded at Marathon (490 BC).
Deiphontes was an Heraclid who took Epidaurus with Argive followers, bringing Dorian settlers who then spread to Ægina.
The Athenian fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami on the Hellespont (405 BC), ending the Athenian hold on Ægina.
"Propitiate" means to appease or win the favour of an angry god; a suppliant is one who humbly begs for help.
"Secretly whispered" means the altar's meaning is only quietly told, a hint of a hidden rite for Æacus.
The pentathlum (pentathlon) was a contest of five events: running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling. The "quoit" is the discus-like throwing weight.
Pausanias compares a story in which Pylades, Orestes' friend, helped kill Neoptolemus; he suggests a family grudge, not only friendship, motivated it.
A "mole" here is a breakwater or causeway of piled stones built out into the sea, not the animal.

context_notes.text: Epidaurus, in Argolis, was famed above all for its sanctuary of Æsculapius, god of healing.
Artemis as a Huntress is the goddess of wild places and hunting.
Ægina was a major Greek sea power, sending ships against Persia at Salamis in 480 BC; Athens expelled its people in 431 BC.
Æacus was the legendary king of Ægina, son of Zeus, famed for justice and piety, and later a judge of the dead.
Delphi's oracle, voiced by the Pythian Priestess of Apollo, was the usual authority Greeks consulted in crises such as drought.
Salamis is the island near Athens that was Telamon's home; his exile from Ægina is the penalty for Phocus' death.

literary_notes.text: The men made from the soil explain the island's population; the autochthonous tale gives the people a divine, native origin.
The sentence traces a sudden reversal of fortune, moving from greatness to expulsion, a pattern common in historical narrative.
Æacus is shown as shrewd and protective, turning the island's natural hazards into a deliberate defence.
The statues of envoys from all Greece symbolize Greek unity and Æacus' piety, as his prayers succeed where others failed.
The hedge "if the Greeks speak the truth" shows Pausanias as a cautious, skeptical reporter of inherited stories.
